image_description: Two adult male mallard ducks (drakes) standing in shallow water. The duck on the left is fully visible, displaying characteristic breeding plumage: iridescent green head, white neck ring, brown chest, and grey body with a blue speculum patch. The duck on the right is partially occluded by the left one but shows similar features. Both have orange webbed feet visible in the water. The background consists of rippling greenish water.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The left drake clearly displays a broad, flat, yellow-green bill consistent with mallard anatomy. The right drake's bill is partially obscured but appears consistent.
The eye of the left drake is clearly visible and dark/black, matching the taxonomy description.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Both subjects exhibit the typical stocky, streamlined duck body shape. Plumage appears dense and structured, not matted or melting.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The left drake perfectly matches the Mallard description: iridescent green head, distinct white neck ring, brown chest, and grey flanks. The color separation is sharp and natural.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Orange legs are visible on both ducks. The feet are clearly webbed with the correct anatomical structure (palmate). No extra toes or fusion artifacts observed.
The folded wings on the left drake show the correct aerodynamic shape and the characteristic blue speculum patch bordered by white stripes.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail of the left drake is visible and shows the characteristic upward curl of the central black feathers, specific to male mallards.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the specific species identification (Mallard) and rule out hybrid or nonsensical bird features.
To verify the structural integrity of the legs and feet, ensuring no fusion with the water or extra limbs.
To check for edge bleeding between the complex feather textures and the water background, a common AI artifact.
To analyze the water ripples for consistency and ensure they do not show 'melting' or repetitive pattern artifacts.

focus_areas: Water ripple physics and texture consistency
custom_prompts_for_reflector: Pay close attention to the interaction between the ducks' feet and the water line. AI often struggles with partial submersion, causing feet to look like they are melting into the water or lacking proper displacement. Also, verify the 'speculum' (blue wing patch) has sharp boundaries and isn't smeared.
